phonemes.desc: Short epsilon with acute pitch stress [é], the rising note that names the darkness.
Rolling rho followed by short epsilon [re], a quick descent between the two peaks.
Voiced bilabial stop [b] plus short omicron and voiceless sigma [bos] — in Classical Attic, beta is still [b], not later [v].

pronunciation.approximation: "EH-reh-BOSS" — first syllable pitched high like 'EH'; second like 'reh'; third like 'boss' with a clear b.
pronunciation.note: Érebos is Tier 2 because Classical Attic Ἔρεβος preserves only stress (acute on the first epsilon), not length. There are no long vowels or diphthongs. The registrable form Érebos keeps the acute accent while remaining DNS-compatible. Note that Classical Attic beta is a voiced stop [b], as Allen reconstructs, not the fricative [v] of later Greek. Sources: Allen, Vox Graeca, 3rd ed. (Cambridge, 1987); LSJ; Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek (Brill, 2010).

domains.title: The Deep Darkness
domains.subtitle: Shadow, Passage, and the Threshold of Death
domains.lead: Érebos is the personification of deep darkness, the shadow that fills the space between earth and Hades. Born directly from Cháos, he is the brother and consort of Nyx, and the father of Aithḗr and Hēméra. His name is both a place and a power: the darkness that the dead must cross, and the primordial shadow from which light first appears.

cards.name: Primordial Darkness
cards.desc: The second offspring of Cháos, older than the Titans, older than the Olympians — the original shadow.

cards.name: The Passage to Hades
cards.desc: The shades of the dead rise from or through Érebos; Odysseus must sail to the edge of the world to reach it.

cards.name: Father of Light
cards.desc: His union with Nyx produces Aithḗr, the bright upper air, and Hēméra, the day — darkness begetting radiance.

cards.name: The Underworld Abyss
cards.desc: In later usage Érebos names the deepest darkness beneath Hades, a region of mist and forgetfulness.

symbols.name: Mist and cloud
symbols.meaning: The mist and cloud that wrap the Cimmerian land at the edge of the world, where the sun never shines (Odyssey 11.13–19)

symbols.name: Consort of black Night
symbols.meaning: Born together with black Nyx, he fathers Aithḗr and Hēméra upon her (Theogony 123–125)

symbols.name: Cavern mouth
symbols.meaning: The entrance to the underworld, often identified with volcanic or marshy places

symbols.name: Shadow
symbols.meaning: The absence of light as a positive, generative power

mythology.lead: Érebos has few independent myths because he is a condition rather than a character — darkness given a genealogy. Yet his appearances are foundational: he is born second of all things from Cháos, he fathers light itself upon Night, and he marks the boundary that every living thing must eventually cross. His mythology is the biography of darkness.

myths.title: The Second Primordial
myths.text: Hesiod opens the Theogony with a sequence that has no author and no maker: first Cháos came to be — the gaping void, the yawn — then broad-bosomed Gaia, then dim Tártaros in the depths, and from Cháos, 'on the same day,' were born Érebos and black Nyx (116–123). West's commentary on the passage stresses what the Greek says plainly: Érebos is not created, and not evil; he is simply second — the second fact of the cosmos after the void itself, the darkness that settles in the space between things before there are things to separate. His pairing with Nyx is exact: Érebos is the darkness that fills the depths, Nyx the night that covers the world above, and the two are born together because they are the two faces of one condition. Later tradition placed him beneath the earth as the dark passage the dead descend; Homer's underworld is wrapped in his gloom. The genealogy is a single claim stated at the very start of Greek literature: before light, before law, before the gods begin their quarrels, there is the shadow that makes all of them visible.

myths.title: Darkness Gives Birth to Light
myths.text: The very next lines of the Theogony (124–125) deliver one of the most elegant genealogies in Greek myth: Nyx, joined with Érebos in love, bore Aithḗr and Hēméra — the bright upper air and the day. It is a paradox engineered into the family tree: the darkest union imaginable produces the radiance that fills the sky and the hours that measure mortal life. The pattern is not conquest — darkness does not fight and lose to light; it emerges from darkness, as children emerge from the night of the womb. Hesiod extends the same rhythm later in the poem (748–757), where he pictures the gates of the abyss and the house of Night and Day standing opposite one another: the two goddesses 'greet each other as they cross the great threshold of bronze' — one descending as the other ascends, forever passing on the same threshold their parents built. The myth encodes the Greek experience of darkness as generative rather than malefic: night and day are sisters, children of the same dark house, and light is what darkness becomes when it is paired with time.

myths.title: The Land Wrapped in Mist
myths.text: Homer gives Érebos his geography. To consult the dead, Odysseus must sail the deep-flowing Ōkeanos to the world's edge, to the land of the Cimmerians, 'wrapped in mist and cloud,' where the sun never looks down — 'neither when he climbs the starry heavens nor when he turns back from heaven toward earth' — and where night and day lie close together (Odyssey 11.13–19). There, at the boundary of Érebos, Odysseus digs the pit, pours the blood, and the shades come up — unmarried youths, old men, warriors still in their bloody gear, and Tiresias, who alone keeps his wits and can answer. The scene is the founding image of the western necromancy: darkness not as punishment but as threshold, the dim antechamber where the living can still question the dead. Kirkē's instructions had warned him not to let the shades taste the blood before Tiresias speaks — even in Érebos, there is protocol. The myth fixes the god's character forever: Érebos is the darkness you cross carefully, with offerings and with questions prepared, because on the far side of it, everyone you have lost is still waiting.

myths.title: Érebos in the Orphic Theogonies
myths.text: The Orphic poets re-worked the Hesiodic primordials into a more intricate cosmogony, and Érebos kept his station near the beginning of things. In the Rhapsodic Theogony as reconstructed from the Neoplatonic summaries, Chronos — Time itself — fashions the cosmic egg in the yawning void of Aithḗr, and from the egg bursts Phanēs, the first creator-god, whose first acts include the making of Nyx; the Orphic theogonies place the powers of darkness, including Érebos, among the deep substrata from which Phanēs arises (West, The Orphic Poems). The Orphic gold tablets — the lamellae buried with initiates from Thessaly to Thurii in southern Italy — send the soul on a journey that rehearses the same geography: past the spring of Memory and the gates of the underworld, through darkness toward light, with the passport line 'I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven' on the dead's own lips. In this tradition Érebos is not merely the place of the dead but the first veil the soul must remember how to cross. The myth's lesson is the mystery-cult's lesson: darkness is the beginning of the journey, not its end.

lore.syncretism: The Romans adopted the Greek name directly as Erebus and deepened it: Virgil places the guilty dead in Tartarus and lets the surrounding darkness swallow the light (Aeneid 6.126–129, where the path into the underworld 'plunges into the darkness, into Erebus's vast gulf'), and Statius makes Erebus a standing synonym for the infernal depths. Christian writers took the word as a classical name for Hell and its antechamber — Milton's Chaos and 'dark Erebus' stand at the threshold of Paradise Lost — and the vocabulary of esotericism later reused Érebos for the primal darkness from which manifestation arises, a notion with deliberate echoes of Kabbalistic tohu wa-bohu and of Neoplatonic accounts of the One beyond being. The name thus travelled from cosmogony to demonology to metaphysics, keeping its spelling and its office: the first dark, in whatever system needs one.
lore.culturalLegacy: Érebos survives as the archetype of primordial darkness. James Clark Ross named Mount Erebus, the active volcano on Ross Island in Antarctica, after one of his ships in 1841 — and the HMS Erebus later became immortal in the disastrous Franklin expedition of 1845, freezing the name into English literature as the emblem of oblivion. Fantasy and science fiction mine it for spaceships, demons, and dark dimensions; astronomy has used it for features on distant moons; heavy metal and horror invoke it as the original shadow. Few Greek names have travelled so far from their cosmogonic origin while keeping the same spelling — and in every stop of the journey, Érebos has meant the same thing: the dark that was there first.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Érebos is the darkness that is not evil. It is simply first. Before light, before form, before the gods begin their quarrels, there is the shadow that makes bright things visible. We moderns tend to moralize darkness — we call it ignorance, despair, or danger — but the Greek primordial is more neutral and more necessary. Without Érebos there is no contrast, no outline, no day.

To restore the acute accent on Érebos is to hear the name as a rising note out of silence. It is the sound of darkness being named rather than feared. Every creation myth needs such a moment: the first word spoken into the void, the first recognition that absence is also a kind of presence.
lore.archaeology: Érebos had no independent cult, but his presence is pervasive in Greek and Roman imaginings of the underworld. The Nekromanteion at Ephyra on the Acheron and the Ploutonion at Hierapolis were entered through passages of darkness and mist. Orphic gold tablets from Thessaly and southern Italy describe the soul's journey through night and shadow toward light. Cosmogonic hymns and astrological papyri from Egypt invoke Érebos as one of the primordial powers. Roman sarcophagi and wall paintings depict the underworld as a realm of deep shadow, often labeled with the names of its Greek precincts.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Greek as Ἔρεβος (Érebos), from the same Indo-European root that gives Sanskrit rájas and Old Norse røkkr. The registrable form Érebos retains the acute accent on the first epsilon, the single prosodic feature preserved in Classical Attic, which places the name in Tier 2. Classical Attic beta is pronounced as a voiced stop [b], so the registrable Latin b accurately represents the ancient sound.
